plan.curriculum: Mathematics 2.0, Measurement, Year 5 (VC2M5M04): measure angles in degrees with a protractor and relate the measures to angle names
plan.shape: example-first: reading a two-scale protractor is new for many, so the teacher models on both scales before any guided measuring
plan.criticalFeature: read the scale that starts at 0 on the arm you lined up
decisionPoints: the choice check on angle names
the hinge: measure with the right scale
plan.anchor: quarter turn 90°, half turn 180°, full turn 360°

manipulatives: A protractor and a ruler for every student
A large demonstration protractor, or the on-screen protractor
studentTools: Printed Worksheet for every student; Extension and Supported Worksheet as needed
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
boardSetup: The anchor on the board: quarter turn 90°, half turn 180°, full turn 360°

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn. Sort, measure and name angles, then sport problems with a mistake to fix.
resources.title: Measuring and Classifying Angles
resources.subtitle: You need a protractor and a ruler.

steps: Compare it with a right angle (90°).
30° is smaller than 90°.
Smaller than 90° is acute.

items.prompt: Write each angle size in the right group. Careful with 89° and 91°!

sections.title: Measure it
sections.intro: If an arm is too short to reach the scale, extend it with your ruler. Then check: does your size match the angle's name?

steps: Put the centre on the corner.
Line up 0 with one arm.
Count up from that 0 to the other arm.

items.prompt: Measure the angle.
Measure the angle.
The arm points left.
Measure the angle.
This one is tilted.
The arm points left.

example.prompt: A goalkeeper's arms make an angle of 110°. Name the angle.
steps: 110° is more than 90°.
110° is less than 180°.
Between 90° and 180° is obtuse.

items.prompt: A skate ramp rises 25° from the ground. Is it steeper or less steep than a ramp at half a right angle? How do you know?
items.answer: Less steep. Half a right angle is 45°, and 25° is less than 45°.

items.prompt: An umpire's arms make a right angle. Which clock time shows the same angle?
items.explain: 3:00: the hands are a quarter turn apart, 90°.

items.prompt: Mia measured this ramp angle. Find her mistake and fix it.
work: I read 130 on the outside row, so the ramp is 130°.
items.answer: It is 50°. The arm is on the right-hand 0, so read the inside row. This angle is acute, not 130°.

items.prompt: A gate is open 100°. The wind blows it open 90° more. How far open is it now? Name the angle.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option. Clock-hand angles, angle riddles and sport problems, with worked examples.
resources.title: Extension: Angle Detectives
resources.subtitle: Use what you know about turns and angle names.

sections.title: Clock angles
sections.intro: A full turn is 360°. A clock has 12 gaps between its numbers, so the hands turn 360° divided by 12 = 30° for each gap.

example.prompt: What angle do the hands make at 2 o'clock?
steps: Count the gaps from 12 to 2: 2 gaps.
Each gap is 30°.
2 × 30° = 60°. That is acute.

items.prompt: Fill in the table. Always use the smaller angle between the hands.
At which two times on the hour do the hands make a right angle? How do you know?
items.answer: 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock: each is 3 gaps from 12, and 3 × 30° = 90°.

example.prompt: I am a multiple of 20. I am obtuse. I am less than 130°. What could I be?
steps: Obtuse means more than 90° and less than 180°.
I must also be less than 130°.
Multiples of 20 in that range: 100 and 120.

items.prompt: I am a multiple of 25. I am obtuse. List everything I could be.
I am a reflex angle and a multiple of 100. What could I be?
Write your own angle riddle that has exactly two answers. Swap with a partner.
items.answer: Check the riddle has exactly two answers, e.g. "I am acute and a multiple of 40": 40° or 80°.

items.prompt: I am half of a straight angle. What am I?
items.explain: A straight angle is 180°, and half of 180° is 90°, a right angle.

example.prompt: A shot leaves at 40°. The coach says make it 15° bigger. What is the new angle? Name it.
steps: Add the change: 40° + 15° = 55°.
55° is less than 90°.
So it is acute.

items.prompt: A footy kick leaves the boot at 35°. The player's next kick is a quarter turn steeper. What is the new angle? Name it.
A diver spins three quarter turns in the air. How far has she turned?

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: For students who need more guidance: protractors printed on, hints on every question.
resources.title: Measuring Angles: Step by Step
resources.subtitle: Take it one step at a time.

example.prompt: What do we call an angle of exactly 90°?
steps: Exactly 90° is a square corner.
A square corner is a right angle.

items.prompt: Finish the name chart.
items.hint: Word bank: acute, obtuse, straight, reflex.

sections.title: Smaller or bigger than a square corner?

steps: Hold the corner of your book on the angle.
The angle is smaller than the corner.
Smaller is acute.

items.prompt: Name this angle.
items.hint: Bigger than the book corner, but not a straight line? Obtuse.

items.prompt: Circle the acute angle.

steps: Find the 0 where the arm lies flat.
Follow that row of numbers up.
Stop where the other arm crosses: 30.

items.prompt: Read this protractor.
items.hint: The arm lies on the right, so start at the 0 on the right.

items.prompt: Read this protractor.
items.hint: It is obtuse, so the answer must be more than 90.

items.prompt: The arm points left. Read this protractor.
items.hint: Start at the 0 on the left.

items.prompt: The arm points left. Read this protractor.
items.hint: Start at the 0 on the left and count up.

slides.notes: Session 1 of our angles week: today we measure angles and name them by their size.
Before you start, put a protractor and a ruler on every desk, with boards and markers. Print the Worksheet for everyone, and a few copies of the Extension and the Supported Worksheet.

slides.title: Fraction, decimal, percentage
prompts: Write 3/4 as a decimal and as a percentage.

beats: SAY: Let's warm up with something from last term:
fractions, decimals and percentages.
ASK: How would you write three quarters as a decimal, and as a percentage?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 0.75 and 75%
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal and move straight on.
Less -> shade the strip: each quarter is 25%. Count them, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: Three quarters is 0.75, which is 75 percent. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 0.34 for three quarters.
Fix: count each quarter as 25%, and they rewrite it.
notes.prep: Daily Review from Term 3 Week 9. Keep the whole review under 6 minutes.

beats: ASK: What is 25 percent of 60?
15 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 15
SCAN boards.
80%+ -> reveal and move on.
Less -> 25% is one quarter, so halve 60, then halve again. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's 15. Twenty-five percent is one quarter,
and a quarter of 60 is 15. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 25 or 35.
Fix: remind them 25% is one quarter, and they halve twice.
notes.prep: Term 3 Week 9 retrieval: a percentage of an amount.

beats: ASK: Can you put these in order from smallest to largest?
30 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
SCAN boards for one half first.
80%+ -> reveal, then on to Fluency.
Less -> change all three to percentages together, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: One half is 50 percent, then 55 percent,
and 0.6 is 60 percent, so it's the biggest. Tick it or fix it.
trap: putting 55% last because 55 looks like the biggest number.
Fix: turn each one into a percentage, and they reorder.
notes.prep: Spaced retrieval from Term 3 Week 5: comparing fractions, decimals and percentages.

slides.title: Add with the written method: 3 digits

beats: SAY: Now for some written addition.
Line up the places, and always start with the ones.
ASK: Use the written method to solve this one.
30 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 825
SCAN boards for the regrouped digits.
80%+ -> reveal, then the next one.
Less -> model the ones and the regroup together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: The answer is 825.
Tick it or fix it, and check every regroup.
trap: forgetting to add a regrouped ten.
Fix: circle each carried digit, and they add that column again.
notes.prep: Addition fluency: 3 digits, then 4, then 5. Keep the whole block under 6 minutes.

slides.title: Add with the written method: 4 digits

beats: SAY: Now it's 4 digits.
It's the same method, just one more column.
ASK: Use the written method to solve this one.
45 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 6 335
SCAN boards for the regrouped digits.
80%+ -> reveal, then the next one.
Less -> model the ones and the regroup together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: The answer is 6 335.
Tick it or fix it, and check every regroup.
trap: forgetting to add a regrouped ten.
Fix: circle each carried digit, and they add that column again.

slides.title: Add with the written method: 5 digits

beats: SAY: Now it's 5 digits.
It's the same method, just one more column.
ASK: Use the written method to solve this one.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 63 512
SCAN boards for the regrouped digits.
80%+ -> reveal, then the learning intention.
Less -> model the ones and the regroup together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: The answer is 63 512.
Tick it or fix it, and check every regroup.
trap: forgetting to add a regrouped ten.
Fix: circle each carried digit, and they add that column again.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to measure angles with a protractor and name them by their size.
successCriteria: I can name an angle as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex.
I can measure an angle by reading the scale that starts at 0.
I can explain how I know my measurement makes sense.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: This week is all about angles.
Today we're learning to measure angles and give them their names.
SAY: Let's read our I can statements together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: We'll start with the names, and then build up to measuring.
By the end, you'll be choosing the right scale every time.
notes.prep: SC1 naming is reachable for everyone; SC2 reading the right scale is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 reasonableness is the stretch.

slides.title: A quarter turn is 90°
slides.prompt: Stand up. Show a quarter turn, a half turn, a full turn.

beats: POINT to the square corner.
SAY: When you make a quarter turn, you make a square corner like this one.
That's 90 degrees.
SAY: Everyone stand up and face the front.
We'll make a quarter turn, then a half turn, then all the way round.
ASK: So how many degrees are a half turn and a full turn?
15 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 180 and 360
SCAN boards for 180 and 360.
80%+ -> write the anchor on the board and move on.
Less -> turn together again, counting 90, 180, 270, 360. Re-ask.
trap: writing 100 for a half turn.
Fix: add two quarter turns, 90 and 90, and they rewrite it.
notes.prep: The launch comes after the LI: everyone moves, then the anchor stays on the board all week. Under 4 minutes.

slides.meaning: A tool for measuring angles in degrees.
slides.example: Put its centre on the corner and read the scale that starts at 0.

notes.answer: a tool for measuring angles in degrees
beats: POINT to the word.
SAY: This is a protractor. Say it with me: protractor.
SAY: We use a protractor to measure angles in degrees.
Look closely and you'll see two rows of numbers going opposite ways.
ASK: Can you point to where the zero is on each row of numbers?
10 sec. Cue: Voices off. Point... now. Hold your point.
EXPECT: one 0 on the right, one 0 on the left
trap: thinking the protractor has only one scale.
Fix: trace each row with a finger until they find both zeros.
notes.prep: The word the whole week depends on. Naming both zeros here sets up the I Do.

slides.title: Name an angle by its size

beats: POINT to right, then straight.
SAY: Let's start with the two angles we know from our turns.
A right angle is a quarter turn, so it's exactly 90 degrees.
A straight angle is a half turn, so it's exactly 180 degrees.
POINT to acute, then obtuse.
SAY: Every other name compares an angle with those two.
Acute is smaller than a right angle.
Obtuse is bigger than a right angle, but not yet a straight line.
POINT to reflex.
SAY: And past a straight line, but short of a full turn, it's reflex.
ASK: If an angle measures 120 degrees, which name would you give it?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: obtuse
trap: calling every angle over 90 obtuse, even reflex ones.
Fix: ask "Is it past 180 too?" and they rewrite the name.
notes.prep: Every name is decided by comparing with the two landmarks, 90 and 180 degrees. SC1.

slides.title: Measure: the arm points right
steps: Put the centre on the vertex.
Line up 0 with one arm.
Count up from that 0 to the other arm.
Check: it is acute, so under 90°.

beats: MODEL the centre on the vertex.
SAY: Let me show you how I measure this one.
First, I put the centre dot right on the corner.
POINT to the inner 0.
SAY: This arm points to the right, so I start at the 0 on the right.
That's the inside row of numbers.
ASK: Count up in tens with me. Where does the other arm cross?
10 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
EXPECT: 65
REVEAL after the choral count.
SAY: It's 65 degrees. That's acute,
so an answer under 90 makes sense.
trap: reading 115 on the outside row.
Fix: finger on the 0 under the arm, and they read it again.
notes.stretch: What does the other row say here? Why do the two readings add to 180?
notes.help: Colour the row of numbers that starts at 0 on your arm.
notes.prep: The key idea: read the scale that starts at 0 on the arm you lined up. SC2.

slides.title: Measure: the arm points left
steps: Put the centre on the vertex.
This arm points left, so use the 0 on the left.
Count up that outer scale to the other arm.
Check: it is obtuse, so between 90° and 180°.

beats: MODEL the centre on the vertex.
SAY: We start the same way: the centre dot on the corner,
and the flat edge along one arm.
POINT to the outer 0.
SAY: This time the arm points to the left,
so I start at the 0 on the left and use the outside row.
ASK: Before we count, is this angle acute or obtuse?
5 sec. Cue: Voices off. One finger for acute, two for obtuse. Show me... now.
EXPECT: two fingers
REVEAL after fingers are scanned.
SAY: It's 125 degrees. It's obtuse,
so an answer between 90 and 180 makes sense.
trap: reading 55 on the inside row.
Fix: ask which 0 sits on the arm, and they count again.
notes.stretch: When could both rows look sensible? How would you choose?
notes.help: Name it first: obtuse means more than 90.
notes.prep: The second model uses the other scale, so the rule is the 0 on your arm, not the inside numbers. SC2 and SC3.

slides.title: Which angle is obtuse?
slides.prompt: Point to A, B or C

options.misconception: calls a right angle obtuse because it looks big
calls any angle over 90° obtuse, even reflex

beats: SAY: Here are three angles.
Check each one against a quarter turn and a half turn.
ASK: Which of these angles is obtuse?
10 sec. Cue: Voices off. Point... now. Hold your point.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then cold call one student: Why isn't it C?
Less -> hold up the name chart, test each against 90 and 180, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: It's B. It's more than a quarter turn,
but less than a half turn.
trap: pointing to C.
Fix: ask whether it's past a half turn, and they rename it reflex.
notes.prep: First decision point: names before measuring. Under 80% means one more pass of the name chart with the turns.

slides.title: Read the protractor
slides.ask: How many degrees is this angle?
slides.pivot: finger on the 0 under the arm, count up in tens
slides.followUp: cold call one board: Which row did you read, and why?

items.say: It's 70 degrees. The arm points left, so we read the outside row.
It's 160, not 20. It's obtuse, so it has to be over 90.

say: Let's practise reading the scale together.
Write each measurement on your board.
trap: reading the row that starts at 180.
Fix: name the angle first, then check the number fits.
notes.stretch: Write both readings for each angle, then circle the real size.
notes.help: Colour the 0 on the arm before you count.
notes.prep: Guided practice on both scales, mixing arms that point right and left. SC2.

beats: SAY: This one is just for you. Measure it on your own.
ASK: How many degrees is this angle?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 48
SCAN every board, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then Your turn.
Less -> rebuild it on the big protractor: centre, 0 on the arm, count up. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's 48 degrees. It's acute,
so an answer under 90 makes sense. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 132.
Fix: ask if it's acute, and they re-read from the 0 on the arm.
notes.prep: The hinge before independent work. Anyone who wrote 132 starts on the Supported Worksheet with the teacher.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.task: Sort, measure and name the angles on your worksheet.

beats: POINT to the steps.
SAY: Read each question carefully, solve it carefully, then check your answers.
SAY: If you finish, the Extension is your early finisher option.
Let's read the steps together. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Check the centre is on the corner and the 0 is on the arm.
TIME: 20 minutes. Stop everyone once at 10 minutes to share a strategy.
trap: the protractor centre is off the corner.
Fix: dot on the corner, and they measure again.
notes.stretch: Extension: clock-hand angles, angle riddles and sport problems, with worked examples.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: protractors printed on the angles, and a hint on every question.
notes.prep: Independent practice, from sorting and measuring to sport problems and reasoning. The sheet is evidence for SC2 and SC3.

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Write the size of this angle and its name.

beats: SAY: Here's the last one. Measure it and name it on your board.
ASK: How many degrees is this angle, and what's its name?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 135, obtuse
RECORD who writes 45, the wrong scale.
They start tomorrow's first check with the teacher.
trap: writing 45.
Fix: none now. Record the name for tomorrow.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 with the arm pointing left, the harder scale. It drives tomorrow's grouping.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Tell your partner how you choose which scale to read.

notes.answer: open - listen for the 0 on the arm
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can statements together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can measure with the right scale?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit board.
A thumb up with 45 on the board matters most.
ASK: Tell your partner how you choose which row of numbers to read.
20 sec. Cue: Partner A first. You have 20 seconds. Go.
EXPECT: the one that starts at 0 on my arm
notes.prep: Read the self-assessment beside the exit evidence. Tomorrow's first check comes from both. SC2.
